segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the assembly of God in Corinth, to those made holy in Christ Jesus, called to be holy people, together with all those who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place, their Lord and ours:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I thank my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given to you in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for in everything you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as the testimony about Christ was made firm among you,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you are not lacking in any gift as you eagerly await the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He will also keep you firm to the end, blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: God is faithful, and through him you were called into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I appeal to you, brothers and sisters, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be fully united in the same mind and the same judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it has been reported to me about you, my brothers and sisters, by Chloe's people, that there are quarrels among you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I mean is this: each of you is saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I belong to Paul,” “I belong to Apollos,” “I belong to Cephas,” “I belong to Christ.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Has Christ been divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized into the name of Paul?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am thankful that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no one can say that you were baptized into my name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I did also baptize the household of Stephanas; beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Christ did not send me to baptize but to announce the good news, and not with wisdom of speech, so that the cross of Christ would not be made empty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the intelligence of the intelligent I will set aside.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where is the wise person? Where is the scholar? Where is the debater of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of the world foolish?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not come to know God through wisdom, God was pleased, through the foolishness of the proclamation, to save those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For Jews ask for signs and Greeks seek wisdom,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God's foolishness is wiser than people, and God's weakness is stronger than people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Consider your calling, brothers and sisters: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, and God chose what is weak in the world to shame what is strong,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and God chose what is lowborn in the world and what is despised, the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that no human being may boast before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But it is from him that you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and holiness and redemption,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that, as it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

notes.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering of citizens and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader hears what the first hearers heard.

The traditional rendering is 'saints', which now suggests exceptional or canonized individuals. Paul uses the word for every member of the community, as people set apart for God. It is from the same root as 'made holy' earlier in the verse, and the rendering keeps that link visible.
The Greek says only 'theirs and ours' and does not say what is shared. Most translations take it with 'Lord', as here. It could instead go with 'place': 'in every place, theirs and ours'.

The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group, and the Corinthian assembly plainly included women. English 'brothers' now reads as men only. More formal translations keep 'brothers' with a footnote saying the word can include women.

Cephas is the Aramaic name ('rock') of the apostle better known by its Greek equivalent, Peter. Paul normally calls him Cephas. Apollos was an eloquent teacher from Alexandria who worked in Corinth after Paul had left (Acts 18:24–19:1).

Most manuscripts read 'I thank God' (some 'my God'). A few of the earliest lack the word 'God', and the SBLGNT follows them, judging that copyists added the familiar phrase. The sense is not materially affected.

The Greek verb was an ordinary word for publicly announcing good news, also used of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' is now a religious term or the name of a book, and 'preach' suggests a sermon. Many modern translations already alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

notes.phrase: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise
notes.note: The quotation is Isaiah 29:14 in its Greek form, with a slight change to the final verb. In Isaiah, God announces that he will confound the political advisers of Judah who rely on their own cleverness.

'Scribe' now suggests a copyist. In Jewish settings the Greek word meant a trained expert in the Scriptures and the law, and most interpreters think Paul sets that figure here beside the Greek sage and the public debater. In Greek cities the same word could also mean a civic secretary, so the reference is not certain. Most translations keep 'scribe'.
The Greek is literally 'so that all flesh may not boast', a Semitic idiom in which 'all flesh' means everyone. The word is the same one rendered 'flesh' in verse 26, and Paul is probably echoing it.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God's action to set things right. Translations into most other languages use a single word for 'justice' throughout, and some scholars prefer 'justice' in English as well.

notes.phrase: Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord
notes.note: This condenses Jeremiah 9:23–24, where the wise, the strong and the rich are told not to boast in their wisdom, strength or wealth but in knowing the Lord. The same passage probably lies behind the list of the wise, the powerful and the well-born in verse 26.

candidates.reason: The plural used of believers recurs in most letters, Acts and Revelation, and translators divide between 'saints', 'holy ones' and 'God's people'; the link to ἁγιάζω and ἁγιασμός ('made holy', 'holiness') also needs one policy.
The plural shifts between 'nations', 'Gentiles' and 'pagans' across the New Testament, and readers should be able to tell it is one Greek word.
Frequent in the Gospels and Acts, where 'scribe' misleads modern readers and alternatives ('scholar', 'legal expert', 'teacher of the law') vary widely.
With its verb σκανδαλίζω it recurs across the Gospels and letters and is rendered variously as 'stumbling block', 'offense', 'trap' or 'cause of sin'.
A favourite Pauline verb, about 25 times, rendered inconsistently ('abolish', 'nullify', 'destroy', 'pass away', 'release') in ways that hide its recurrence in key arguments.
